newsitem.title: UK: Britain on course for full employment by 2000. [CORRECTED 12:41 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Britain on course for full employment by 2000. [CORRECTED 12:41 GMT]

text.p: Britain is well on the way to becoming one of just three European Union countries to enjoy full employment, possibly by the the turn of the century.

Economists, who define full employment as a jobless rate of five percent or less, expect British unemployment to fall steadily from the November rate of 6.9 percent and say Britain could soon join Luxembourg and Austria at the top of the European jobs league table.

"At the present rate unemployment is falling, I would be very surprised if the rate didn't fall below five percent -- which in economic terms is full employment -- within the next three years," said Kevin Gardiner, an economist at Morgan Stanley.
"The actual numbers leaving unemployment are not as high as we are led to believe, but plenty of jobs are being created and being filled."

Britain's unemployment rate compares with rates of around three percent in Luxembourg and 4.1 percent in Austria -- but it is considerably better than France's 12.7 percent, Italy's 12.2 percent and the new post-war high of 10.8 percent reported in Germany on Thursday.

British unemployment plunged an unprecedented 95,800 in November to 1.929 million, the sharpest fall on record. It was the first time since 1991 that it had gone below the psychologically important two million level.
Most analysts believe these figures exaggerated the trend and were distorted by the introduction of a new "job seekers' allowance" and changes in rules on means testing for benefits.
But all agree the underlying trend is positive.

"Consumer confidence is on a rising trend (Corrects to "on a rising trend" from "set to skyrocket") and this will have a positive impact on the economy, which in itself will create even more jobs," said David Owen of Kleinwort Benson, adding that he would not be surprised if the jobless rate dipped to around six (Corrects from five) percent over the next three years.
Structural changes in the labour market have encouraged the creation of new jobs, although many of these may be short-term.
"Because of the limited power of the trade unions in Britain, companies are now a lot less afraid to hire and fire employees and this has led to a greater turnover in the work force," Owen said.

"There are lots of insecure jobs and contracts being offered on a short term basis. My prediction is that unemployment will fall to below 1.8 million by the end of 1997 and this positive trend will continue until the turn of the century."
Gardiner said all the elements are in place for a continued fall in unemployment.

The labour supply is not expanding very rapidly, the economy is expected to show steady growth and productivity is likely to remain relatively constant. He sees unemployment below six percent by 1998, with further falls likely by 2000.
Kit Juckes of NatWest Capital Markets believes unemployment could fall to as low as six percent by the end of this year.

"I am by no means surprised at the downward trend in unemployment, even taking into account the fact that the figures are distorted by the job seekers allowance and that the numbers entering the labour force are decreasing because of the high percentage of school leavers entering universities," he said.
"There is no denying that unemployment is falling and will continue to fall. By the end of this year, I predict it will be close to six percent, with under 1.75 million people in Britain unemployed."
GDP could grow by around 3.75 percent this year and this will create jobs. "Even if these jobs are short term in a changing labour market, a job is still a job," Juckes said.
